summary: Where things are: عَلَى (on), تَحْتَ (under), بِجَانِبِ (next to), أَمَامَ (in front of), خَلْفَ / وَرَاءَ (behind), بَيْنَ … وَ… (between … and …), دَاخِلَ / خَارِجَ (inside / outside), all followed by the genitive; قَرِيبٌ مِنْ (near) and بَعِيدٌ عَنْ (far from) are adjectives that agree with the subject; عَلَى الْيَمِينِ / عَلَى الْيَسَارِ = on the right / on the left. The sentence needs no verb: الْكِتَابُ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ (the book is on the table). For “there is a …” the place comes first and the indefinite noun after it: عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ. Most of these words are old nouns in the accusative (تَحْتَ “the place below”, أَمَامَ “the front”): that is why they end in -a, take a genitive, and take the pronoun endings — تَحْتَهُ, أَمَامَكَ, خَلْفِي. Unlike German, Arabic does not change the case for “where to?”.

blocks.caption: A place word + a genitive noun; no verb “to be” is needed.

items.title: there is a … on …
points: the place first, then the new thing (indefinite, nominative)
هَلْ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ؟ — is there a book on the table?

blocks.caption: The same endings as on nouns and on فِي, مِنْ … : عَلَى → عَلَيْ- (like إِلَى), وَرَاءَ → وَرَائِي (the hamza moves onto a yāʾ seat before -ī).

blocks.title: Near and far agree.
blocks.text: قَرِيب and بَعِيد are adjectives: الْبَنْكُ قَرِيبٌ, but الْمَدْرَسَةُ قَرِيبَةٌ, الْقَرْيَةُ بَعِيدَةٌ. They take a preposition: قَرِيبٌ مِنْ …, بَعِيدٌ عَنْ … (or مِنْ).

blocks.title: بَيْنَ with pronouns is repeated.
blocks.text: بَيْنَ الْبَيْتِ وَالْمَدْرَسَةِ — but بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ (between you and me): before a pronoun ending بَيْنَ is said again.

blocks.title: Inside / outside.
blocks.text: With a noun: دَاخِلَ الْبَيْتِ, خَارِجَ الْبَيْتِ (+ genitive). Without a noun: فِي الدَّاخِلِ (inside, indoors), فِي الْخَارِجِ (outside — and also “abroad”).

blocks.title: Rooms are constructs.
blocks.text: غُرْفَةُ النَّوْمِ (bedroom), غُرْفَةُ الْجُلُوسِ (living room): the case ending is on the first word — فِي غُرْفَةِ النَّوْمِ, بَيْنَ غُرْفَةِ النَّوْمِ وَالْمَطْبَخِ. German makes one word (Schlafzimmer), Arabic two.
No Wechselpräpositionen: German says auf dem Tisch (where?) but auf den Tisch (where to?); Arabic keeps عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ in both, always with the genitive.

askYourself: Which relation do I need: on, under, next to, in front, behind, between, inside, outside, near, far?
Is the thing known (the …)? → thing first: الْكِتَابُ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ. New (a …, there is)? → place first: عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ.
Is the noun after the place word in the genitive (-i / -in)?
Near / far: does قَرِيب / بَعِيد agree with the subject, and did I add مِنْ / عَنْ?
Between: بَيْنَ X وَ Y — with pronouns repeat بَيْنَ.
A pronoun after the place word? → the ending: عَلَيْهِ, تَحْتَهَا, أَمَامَكَ.

traps: *كِتَابٌ عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ for “there is a book on the table” — say عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ كِتَابٌ.
“Near the house” is قَرِيبٌ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ, not *قَرِيبٌ الْبَيْتَ.
تَحْتَ, أَمَامَ, خَلْفَ end in -a; بِجَانِبِ ends in -i (it contains بِـ).

quiz.why: Subject nominative (-u), the noun after عَلَى genitive (-i); no verb.

quiz.q: “There is a bag under the bed.”
quiz.why: An indefinite subject comes after the place: تَحْتَ السَّرِيرِ حَقِيبَةٌ.
قَرِيب agrees with the feminine subject and takes مِنْ.
With pronoun endings بَيْنَ is repeated.
“On the right / left” is عَلَى الْيَمِينِ / عَلَى الْيَسَارِ.
With a noun: دَاخِلَ (-a) + genitive; فِي الدَّاخِلِ stands alone.

quiz.q: German: auf dem Tisch (where?) / auf den Tisch (where to?). Arabic?
quiz.why: Arabic has no “two-way” prepositions: the noun after عَلَى is always genitive.

seeAlso.note: The Hebrew words are often the same Semitic words: עַל = عَلَى, תַּחַת = تَحْتَ, בֵּין = بَيْنَ; Hebrew לְיַד (“by the hand of”) is “next to” where Arabic says بِجَانِبِ (“at the side of”).
German two-way prepositions take the dative for “where?” (auf dem Tisch) and the accusative for “where to?” (auf den Tisch); Arabic always has the genitive: عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ.
Chinese puts the place word after the noun — 桌子上 (table-on), 床下 (bed-under), 在桌子上; Arabic puts it before: عَلَى الطَّاوِلَةِ, تَحْتَ السَّرِيرِ.
Every place word is followed by the genitive (lesson 11).
